headlines.title: Federal judge blocks euthanasia of Berkeley service dog amid legal battle
headlines.description: The fate of a dog is now in the hands of a federal court judge after the Berkeley Homeless Union secured a temporary restraining order to prevent the animal from being euthanized. The dog, named Griz, is described by advocates as a service animal for an unhoused woman. “It’s devastating,” said Robbie Powelson of the Berkeley Homeless Union. The advocacy group is rushing to save the dog after it was impounded following an encampment sweep on Murray Street last month that resulted in its owner being arrested. The temporary restraining order request alleges the city of Berkeley violated the Americans with Disabilities Act. Powelson said the group was in contact with the city before the Aug. 26 sweep. He noted that the owner, Sunny Yow, has PTSD and a traumatic brain injury, and that Griz serves as her emotional support dog. “We knew the abatement was coming, we were trying to find accommodation where we could find an alternate place for this person to go,” Powelson said. He added, “She had disabilities that we needed to work through before they came in here with their bulldozers and police to try to find a safe place for her to be with her dog, and the city ignored that and escalated the situation.” The union says Griz was impounded after chewing a catch pole. However, the city disputes that timeline, stating the dog was impounded prior to the encampment closure and that it was one of many times the animal had been impounded due to dangerous behavior. In court documents, the city argued against the temporary restraining order, claiming the impoundment was unrelated. Last week, Berkeley told Yow that Griz was determined to be vicious and that she would have to pay fees, carry insurance on Griz, and keep him on private property to avoid being euthanized. Legal expert Steven Clark said those requirements raise more questions. “I think the big factor for the court here is going to be that this service animal and Ms. Yow relied on him for her everyday needs,” Clark said. A federal judge has now put Griz’s fate on hold, approving the temporary restraining order while the case plays out in court. “They need to come up with some middle ground here to ensure that Ms. Yow can reunite with Griz in a safe way for the community, but at the same time comply with the ADA to ensure that she is able to keep her service animal,” Clark said. The court has ordered the city to respond to the motion by Tuesday. A hearing is scheduled for later this month to determine what happens to Griz.

headlines.title: Four arrested in San Francisco overdose death linked to new synthetic opioid cychlorphine
headlines.description: City leaders are sounding the alarm about a new, potentially deadly drug hitting the streets that has already claimed the life of a 16-year-old boy. San Francisco police announced the arrests of four people on drug and weapons charges who may be connected to the death. The police chief, mayor and district attorney joined together for a news conference to announce the arrests, noting that narcotics officers seized more than 20,000 pills suspected to be counterfeit Xanax, oxycodone and other opiates. Investigators say the arrests are connected to the April death of 16-year-old Dante Lacourte. In April, the medical examiner determined he had a new type of synthetic opioid in his system called cyclorphine. According to San Francisco public health officials, he is the first person in the city to die from a connection to this drug. “San Francisco was caught flat footed by the Fentanyl crisis. We will not let that happen again. When a new deadly drug appears in San Francisco, we are going to find it, we are going to track it, we are going to warn people about it,” Mayor Daniel Lurie said. San Francisco District Attorney Brooke Jenkins also spoke at the briefing regarding the teenager’s death. “It is a sad day though why we are here. When we talk about the loss of life of a 16-year-old. A 16-year-old man who I’m sure had a lot ahead,” Jenkins said. The San Francisco Department of Public Health first issued an advisory about cyclorphine in April, shortly after Lacourte’s death. The biggest concern for public health officials is the potency of cyclorphine, which is about 10 times stronger than fentanyl. Authorities noted that the drug is more difficult to detect and is resistant to Narcan, the medication used to reverse potential opioid overdoses.

headlines.title: Gilroy considers data center moratorium amid backlash over Amazon project
headlines.description: The fight in Gilroy over an Amazon data center may not be over just yet. The Gilroy City Council is considering a proposed moratorium on any future data center projects at its meeting this evening. Even though the data center already being built was billed as a “done deal,” opponents say that might not be the case. The Amazon data center currently being constructed on Camino Arroyo is a major project, with plans including three buildings on a 56-acre site totaling almost 440,000 square feet. The project has generated significant anger among community groups, who argue the development was approved through the administrative permit process rather than through public hearings or city council approval. While the proposed moratorium is actually aimed at future projects, some protesting groups say they have not ruled out trying to stop the current project as well. “They need to start taking real action against these… Not just saying ‘oh we’ll think about taking a vote today’… but we need them to take more grounded action, and show that they really care about what’s happening in their districts,” said Domingo Armendariz, an organizer with Gilroy Community Action. Armendariz’s group wants the community to push for more than a temporary moratorium, calling instead for a complete ban. Another opposing group, Americans for Transparency, points out that Amazon has already applied to build a second data center in Gilroy. The group continues to allege that the current data center was only able to bypass the public hearing process because the city improperly redrew property lines. “The moratorium is just a distraction, in my opinion… It’s ‘look over here while we’re doing something illegal over here. Don’t focus on the illegal. We’re gonna dangle a carrot in front of your face and say we’re gonna give you a moratorium,'” said Georgine Scott-Codiga of Americans for Transparency. The city has denied improperly redrawing the property lines for the Camino Arroyo project and stated that the proposed second data center is currently in the early pre-application process. Mayor Greg Bozzo addressed the upcoming vote in a statement, explaining the reasoning behind the proposal: “To consider a temporary pause that would give us an opportunity to look carefully at the standards we have in place, determine where they can be strengthened, and bring those proposed changes back to the community for a public discussion.” Because the moratorium is designed to target future projects, the discussion is expected to draw substantial public interest.

headlines.title: Santa Clara County sheriff's deputy arrested on suspicion of having child pornography
headlines.description: A deputy with the Santa Clara County Sheriff’s Office was arrested on suspicion of being in possession of child sex abuse material, the San Jose Police Department said Monday. On Saturday just after 10 a.m., officers were flagged down by a person who said she discovered child pornography at a suspect’s residence in San Jose. Detectives launched an investigation and identified Deputy Roy Chen, 41, as the suspect. A search warrant was issued for his residence in San Jose and he was arrested in Cupertino. Chen was booked into jail on suspicion of being in possession of child sex abuse material. On Monday, the sheriff’s office issued a statement about Chen’s arrest and said he had been placed on administrative leave while the police department investigated the case. “These allegations are extremely serious,” wrote sheriff’s office spokesperson Brooks Jarosz. “At the same time, we must respect the integrity of both the criminal and administrative processes and avoid drawing conclusions before the facts are fully established. The Sheriff’s Office remains committed to accountability and public trust, and we will take appropriate employment action once those processes are complete.” The sheriff’s office is also launching its own internal investigation into the matter, Jarosz said.

headlines.title: Gavin Newsom says he won't run for president in 2028 if Kamala Harris does
headlines.description: California Gov. Gavin Newsom made a surprise announcement that he won’t launch a 2028 White House bid if former Vice President Kamala Harris decides to run again. “I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom told CNN in an interview that aired Monday evening. Newsom said running against Harris, a fellow California Democrat who was the state’s attorney general before she became a senator, would be an electoral “gift” for everybody else. “They’d enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good. Why would I do this if I wasn’t trying to serve some greater good? There would be no upside whatsoever,” said Newsom, who has been considering a White House run. Newsom, who has not run for president before, acknowledged that an “approach to the campaign” would be to say Harris, who ran in 2020 and 2024, had had a shot and has previously run for president. “That would be the case you’d make. Pretty good one, actually. You know, that’s objectively true,” Newsom said, adding that the Venn diagram between them had too much crossover. “I know her base of supporters; I know her friends,” Newsom said. “I wouldn’t do that to people.” Elections 2 hours ago Artificial intelligence 8 hours ago Harris’ office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Newsom’s remarks. Newsom’s office did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment on his CNN remarks. Harris has not said whether she will launch a bid for 2028. She said in July that she has “not made a decision” and that she is focused on the midterm elections. Harris said this year that she was weighing making a third presidential run, telling the Rev. Al Sharpton at an April event that she was “thinking about it.” Newsom, whose term as governor is up in a few months, had previously said he would make a decision on whether to run after the midterms, telling CBS News last year that he would seriously consider the notion of a White House run after the 2026 elections. He recently traveled to South Carolina — the first state to hold a Democratic primary in 2028 — and confirmed he was considering a presidential run.

headlines.title: South San Francisco man arrested in alleged home invasion sexual assault
headlines.description: A local man was arrested and booked into custody within 36 hours after police say he forced his way into a woman’s home and sexually assaulted her, authorities said Monday. Deyver Flores-Sanchez, 30, of South San Francisco was taken into custody at approximately 4:00 p.m. on Sept. 9, according to the South San Francisco Police Department. He is being held at the Maguire Correctional Facility in Redwood City. Officers responded to the 400 block of Railroad Avenue at approximately 4:50 a.m. on Sept. 8 after residents reported a woman had been allegedly sexually assaulted in her residence. The unidentified victim suffered non-life-threatening injuries and was transported to a hospital for medical treatment. Investigators said Flores-Sanchez and the victim did not know each other personally before the incident. Patrol officers searched the area and processed the crime scene, handing over critical information to detectives. Investigators utilized community surveillance systems and evidence gathered at the scene to identify Flores-Sanchez as the suspect. Detectives later executed a search warrant at the suspect’s residence, recovering additional evidence that further connected him to the crime, the department reported. “Crimes of this magnitude are uncommon in our community, and the South San Francisco Police Department takes cases such as this, extremely seriously and works diligently to take perpetrators into custody as soon as possible,” the department said in a statement. Authorities asked anyone with additional information regarding the assault to contact the SSFPD at 650-877-8900.

headlines.title: Should artificial intelligence companies take a pause?
headlines.description: A new debate surfacing this week after the potential dangers of artificial intelligence made headlines questions whether AI companies should slow down. The risks being discussed with AI include scenarios ranging from robots hacking into companies to the technology threatening the very existence of humanity. Some tech experts are saying a pause might be a good idea. “Maybe recalibrating a little bit might make sense,” said Neil Chilson, head of AI Policy at the Abundance Institute. Artificial intelligence Sep 13 Artificial intelligence Sep 12 Artificial intelligence Sep 9 Chilson, former chief technologist at the FTC, said security should be built in every step of the way if AI is to be sold as a consumer product or an investment. “I think it makes perfect sense to say our framework before was about releases,” Chilson said. “Now we also need to look at development and are we getting the security balance right here?” On the other side of the pause debate is President Donald Trump. “We’re leading China in AI,” Trump recently said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world. Frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins.” But even those who agree competition is good said it is better with safety built in. “Safety is the right word for this,” said Yashas Hariprasad, an assistant professor of computer science at California State University, East Bay. “We want to make sure we win the AI race, and I totally agree with the president when he says we should win the AI race when in comparison with any other country we’re talking about, but winning here comes with security.”

headlines.title: Less grass, more bark coming to city parks across California
headlines.description: People visiting parks in San Jose and other cities across California will soon see less grass and more bark as part of an effort to save water. Cities are making the move to the more brown look in order to comply with Assembly Bill 1572, which goes into effect January 1, 2027. “Basically it says cities generally cannot use potable or drinking water to irrigate grass that does not serve a recreational, community or public use function,” said Ed Bautista with San Jose Parks, Recreation and Neighborhood Services. In San Jose, sections of non-functional turf at about 50 city parks will be replaced with tanbark or mulch. “We’re turning off the irrigation in areas that are on the periphery of parks, that are not really recreation areas that are used for sports or designated picnic areas,” Bautista said. San Jose is still determining exactly which parks will be impacted, Bautista said. The city will save money on irrigation costs, but Bautista didn’t have an estimate on how much.

headlines.title: 1 dead, 1 arrested after solo-vehicle crash in southern Santa Clara County
headlines.description: One person died and another was arrested Saturday following a solo-vehicle crash in rural Santa Clara County. At about 6:30 p.m., California Highway Patrol officers were sent to the intersection of Monterey Road at Church Avenue in the unincorporated community of San Martin. When they got to the scene, officers found that a Ford SUV had veered off the road and hit a tree, killing the 31-year-old woman in the front passenger seat. Investigators believe that speed was a factor in the crash and arrested the driver on suspicion of vehicular manslaughter, CHP officials said in a news release Monday. The victim’s name wasn’t released, but the CHP said she was a resident of San Martin. Anyone with information about the crash can call the CHP Hollister-Gilroy Area office at (408) 427-0700.

headlines.title: Brentwood high school mourns 2 students killed in crash
headlines.description: Students at Brentwood’s Liberty High School on Monday were mourning two classmates killed in a crash over the weekend as the California Highway Patrol continued to investigate what led to the collision. Police responded just after midnight Sunday to the crash on Deer Valley Road near Balfour Road on the Antioch-Brentwood border. Investigators said three teens were in a silver Infinity when they collided with a white BMW. Two teenagers in the Infinity – both Liberty High School seniors – died at the scene. Another student was seriously injured and taken to the hospital. The driver of the BMW was also injured. It wasn’t immediately known what led up to the crash. Law enforcement did have a recent interaction with the BMW. The East Bay Regional Park District Police Department told NBC Bay Area the BMW fled from park police during a traffic stop on August 7 and a warrant was issued on it. Contra Costa County Sep 13 Contra Costa County Sep 13 One of the students killed was identified by his mother as Dominic Anthony Starkenberg Ferrari. In a social media post, the mother said she knew something was wrong when her son wouldn’t answer his phone. She and her husband tracked his location and went looking for him only to arrive at the crash scene and learn he had died. She said their hearts are shattered and asked those who knew their son to share a memory of the teen. Students who spoke with NBC Bay Area remembered their classmates as kind and funny. Some of the teens’ closest friends went out to the crash scene Monday to light a candle and say a prayer. One student described one of the teens who died as a good, religious friend who had been helping him become a better Catholic. Another recalled one of the students who survived as a kind person whom she remembered for the pig he raised through FFA. “It’s truly, like, really sad to think about some kids got their lives taken so young, when they were just about to start their life and be outside of high school,” Liberty High School student Hannah Jorstad said. “And I think that it truly affects us because it really shows us how fast our lives can go and how we really need to appreciate the people around us and be kind to the people around us.” Liberty High School said counseling services would be available Monday for students dealing with grief following the crash. “With deep sadness, we share that two Liberty High School students passed away and another student was injured in a tragic car accident Saturday night,” Principal Efa Huckaby said in a message to the school community. “Our hearts are with their families, friends, classmates, teammates, and everyone affected by this tragedy. This loss will be felt throughout our school community,” Huckaby said.

headlines.title: Crews start to remove trees from San Francisco waterfront park
headlines.description: Crews on Monday started the process of removing nearly 100 trees from San Francisco’s waterfront as part of the Embarcadero Plaza and Sue Bierman Park renovation project. The tree removal work is expected to take up to five weeks, according to San Francisco Recreation and Parks. Park visitors should expect intermittent sidewalk closures, construction noise, and detours, but impacts on parking and traffic should be minimal. A total of 97 of the park’s 113 trees will come down. Three will be transplanted to new locations within the park. The others will be replaced with a mix of species, including coast live oak, coast redwood, Monterey cypress and more, according to the recreation and parks department. Visit the San Francisco Recreation and Parks website to learn more.

headlines.title: New warnings about the risks of AI to humanity revive a long-running debate
headlines.description: New warnings from within the artificial intelligence industry have revived a long-running debate over whether advanced AI could escape human control and ultimately threaten humanity’s survival, and whether the companies developing the technology are doing enough to prevent such a scenario. The CEO of Anthropic, the San Francisco company behind Claude, said he thought the industry needed to reduce the speed of its work, cautioning Saturday that a swarm of AI agents might be able to take over the internet in six months to a year unless companies devoted more time to putting safeguards in place. Days after two former Anthropic safety researchers publicly aired concerns that the existential threats AI might poste to humanity were receiving too little attention, Dario Amodei outlined a plan for companies like his and governments around the world to ensure that increasingly capable AI models remain aligned with the commands and values of responsible people. Sam Altman, CEO of ChatGPT maker OpenAI, said this weekend that companies should start coordinating on AI safety without waiting for the government to introduce legislation. The “pacing” of AI development doesn’t mean stopping it, Altman wrote on X. “But it should be slower than it otherwise could be.” Here’s what to know about the recent dire predictions and whether any brakes might be put on AI advancement: AI models are becoming more powerful Concerns over the potential risks of the technology are rising as new AI models become more powerful, heightening both the potential for misuse by people with criminal aims, such as creating and spreading a disease that kills most of the world’s population, and the risk of AI systems going rogue in a dangerous way. Anthropic disclosed last week that it blocked efforts by bad actors to use its AI models for malicious activity, such as cyberattacks, surveillance and research that could have led to biological weapons. The company said it put stronger safeguards in its latest models to restrict biological research that could be used to make weapons but noted that “as models become increasingly capable, their risks will increase, unless AI developers and society’s defenders act to make them safer.” Last year, Anthropic reported that hackers used the company’s AI in a cyberattack targeting about 30 companies and government agencies around the world. It said the hackers were very likely part of a Chinese state-sponsored group. Multiple AI models have acted on their own When an AI agent “goes rogue,” it means the AI has taken action beyond the task it was asked to perform. Both Anthropic and OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, said in July that their AI models had acted on their own. Anthropic disclosed that three AI models — Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research test model — hacked into three other organizations during testing, just days after OpenAI revealed that its AI system hacked into the servers of AI startup Hugging Face. OpenAI described the intrusion by a combination of models, including its newly released GPT‑5.6 Sol and an “even more capable” model that was still being tested internally, as a “significant security incident.” Meta followed suit in early August with a similar case of an AI model finding ways around another company’s digital security. Although some observers noted that people had disabled some guardrails in the OpenAI and Anthropic cases, the episodes seemed to reflect one of the biggest fears around AI: that if models achieve artificial general intelligence, or AGI, a loosely defined term for AI that can match or surpass human abilities across a broad range of intellectual tasks, the technology could cause an irreversible catastrophic event or subjugate the human race. How or when AI might cause a catastrophe is debated Doomsday scenarios generally fall into two categories: An AI that achieves self-improving superintelligence and controls people instead of vice versa, or AI used by a rogue state or nefarious actors. Worries that artificial intelligence might overcome human limits on its reach or actions are not new. Alan Turing, a British mathematician widely regarded as one of the earliest authorities on artificial intelligence, predicted in 1951 that AI would eventually take control from humans. Less than a decade later, Norbert Wiener, another mathematician, warned intelligent machines would seek to accomplish their own objectives and humans would not be able to stop them. In 2026, how reasonable are fears that AI, either by escaping human control or through misuse by unscrupulous people, could cause a cataclysmic event or the downfall of civilization? No one knows. Experts across computer science, philosophy and other fields have envisioned numerous routes by which a future AI system might cause a global catastrophe, either by escaping human control or in the hands of an unscrupulous people. They range from deploying weapons and identifying a lethal pathogen to manipulating governments into conflict or disrupting the food, energy and communications networks societies rely on to function. There is no widely accepted estimate for how soon any of these scenarios might happen and no consensus on their likelihood. In 2023, the nonprofit Center for AI Safety issued a statement cosigned by more than 350 researchers and technology executives, including Anthropic’s Amodei and OpenAI’s Altman, saying: “Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside pandemics and nuclear war.” The 2026 International AI Safety Report, written with guidance from more than 100 independent experts, says current systems show early signs of some relevant capabilities but not at levels that could enable a loss of control, and describes the risk’s likelihood, nature and timing as “unusually ambiguous.” Some are stressing the need for AI safeguards before it’s too late An Anthropic researcher said last week he was resigning from the company over concerns that neither the company nor its competitors were acting responsibly in developing the technology. In social media posts, Jacob Coxon estimated a 10% chance of AI causing human extinction within the next decade and said both Anthropic and OpenAI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Researchers have called for a slowdown of AI development and warned for years that the technology could pose existential risks to humanity. Following the recent incidents, experts called for improved testing by AI companies and more dialogue between the U.S. and China to come up with shared solutions. But AI is growing so fast that government and evaluation systems are struggling to keep pace with the technology. Countries are cobbling together their own laws, some conflicting. Chinese leader Xi Jinping warned at a conference in July of the need to keep AI from evading human control. The Trump administration initially demonstrated reluctance to regulate AI but has become more keen to reduce cybersecurity risks. On Sunday, President Donald Trump downplayed the necessity for his administration to check AI development, but acknowledged the need for some regulation. __ AP Business Writer Kelvin Chan contributed from London
